<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README provided, it is clear that Jesse is an advanced, modular algorithmic trading framework built in Python. Its purpose is to let users quickly research, build, backtest, optimize, and even live‐trade their own crypto trading strategies. Given its diverse codebase—with components for strategies, indicators, exchange integration, data storage, various modes (backtest, optimization, import candles, etc.), and even UI assets—the system design diagram needs to capture multiple layers and interactions.

Below are detailed guidelines for creating a detailed system design/architecture diagram tailored to Jesse:

1. Identify the Main Components:
 a. Trading Engine Core
  • Core logic and configuration – e.g., jesse/config.py, jesse/info.py.
  • Strategy handling – the “jesse/strategies” module which defines trading strategies and business rules.
  • Execution and order management – modules found in jesse/factories, jesse/models, and jesse/services (for order creation, trade execution, logging, metrics, and risk management).
 b. Data/State Management Layer
  • The “jesse/store” directory which holds various state modules (candles, completed trades, orders, positions, tickers, etc.).
  • “jesse/models” which defines persistent data structures.
  • Services for database/cache interactions in “jesse/services/db” and “jesse/services/redis.”
 c. Market Data & Exchange Integration
  • “jesse/exchanges” and its submodules (including sandbox drivers) represent the connectors to external crypto exchanges. They include drivers for different exchanges (Binance, Bybit, Coinbase, etc.).
  • The controllers (in jesse/controllers) that may fetch or display exchange info.
 d. Indicators and Analytics
  • The “jesse/indicators” module (a large directory with many individual technical indicators).
  • Research utilities in “jesse/research” that support backtesting and analysis.
 e. Modes & Pipeline Management
  • Jesse supports different modes such as “backtest_mode”, “optimize_mode”, “import_candles_mode” (in jesse/modes) that govern how strategies are simulated or optimized.
  • Each mode acts as a pipeline that takes in market data, applies strategies/indicators, and then produces orders.
 f. User Interface and External Dependencies
  • “jesse/static” and the attached assets (including the nuxt-monaco-editor assets) suggest that there is a built-in code editor/dashboard or web UI interface.
  • This layer may be used both during live trading (alerts, real-time visualization) and for debugging during simulation.

2. Determine Relationships and Interactions:
 • Data Flow: Market data captured from external exchanges (via the exchange drivers) is converted into candles and then stored/processed by the data layer.
 • Strategy Evaluation: The engine loads user-defined strategies from the “jesse/strategies” directory. Within the current time‐frame (and using indicators from “jesse/indicators”), it derives trading signals.
 • Order Execution: When signal conditions trigger, the trading engine (via factories and service modules) creates orders that are sent through the exchange connectors.
 • State Updates: Order executions and trade results update the internal “store” (state modules), and models that might be used in subsequent strategy evaluations.
 • Modes and Pipelines: Backtesting mode simulates the above flow against historical data, while optimize mode adjusts parameters; each mode interacts with the core engine and data layer.
 • UI and Debugging Tools: The static assets and embedded code editor connect to the live engine (via RESTful APIs or socket services implemented in “jesse/services/web” and “jesse/routes”) to visualize performance, metrics, and logs.

3. Architectural Patterns and Principles:
 • Modularity: The tree shows distinct modules (exchanges, strategies, indicators, models, services, etc.) that follow a plug‑and‑play design so that new strategies, indicators, or drivers can be added easily.
 • Separation of Concerns: For example, separation between strategy logic (“jesse/strategies”), data processing (store and models), and exchange connectivity (exchange drivers) is evident.
 • Pipeline or Microservice-like Breakdown: Different “modes” (backtest, optimize, import candles) are organized as self-contained pipelines that operate atop the same core engine.
 • Extensibility: The sheer number of files in “indicators”, “strategies”, and even in “modes/import_candles_mode/drivers” shows that extensibility was a primary design goal.

4. Technologies and Frameworks:
 • Python is the primary language.
 • There is integration with Docker (Dockerfile, .dockerignore) and GitHub workflows, indicating CI/CD practices.
 • The nuxt-monaco-editor assets in the static folder suggest frontend integration (likely with Nuxt.js/Vue) for the code editor or web UI.
 • Testing frameworks are in place (see “tests” directory).

5. Diagram Construction Guidelines:
 a. Use a layered diagram that separates:
  – The External Market Data & Exchange layer (exchange drivers, API connectors).
  – The Core Trading Engine with submodules for strategy evaluation, order management, risk management, and indicator analysis.
  – The Data/State Persistence layer (stores, models, databases/cache).
  – The Modes (backtesting, optimization, candle-import) that orchestrate the flow.
  – The UI/Integration layer (REST API services, web routes, static assets).
 b. Draw directional arrows that show how data flows:
  – From external exchanges (data input) to the engine.
  – From the engine to the data store and back into strategy computation.
  – From strategy outputs to order execution and updating state.
  – From the internal engine out to user interfaces and dashboards.
 c. Use color coding or different shapes to differentiate:
  – Service layers (e.g., rectangles for modules such as “Strategies”, “Indicators”, “Exchanges”).
  – Data stores (cylinders or databases icons).
  – UI components (e.g., rounded boxes or cloud shapes).
  – External integrations (icons representing APIs or external exchanges).
 d. Label each component clearly with its name and a brief function
  – For example, “Strategies (jesse/strategies): user-defined trading logic” or “Indicators (jesse/indicators): technical analysis library.”
  – Highlight how each subsystem communicates, whether via direct function calls or through an event-driven mechanism.

6. Tailor the Diagram to Jesse’s Purpose:
 – Emphasize that while Jesse is not a traditional “full-stack” web application, it does combine back-end trading logic with front-end interfaces.
 – Highlight the flow starting from market data ingestion, processing with strategy and risk management, then order generation and execution, and finally state updates displayed on the UI.
 – Capture the ecosystem around testing (from the “tests” folder) to denote that robust quality assurance methods are part of the design.

7. Final Recommendations:
 • Ensure your diagram does not merely break the system into “just boxes” but shows clear interdependencies – for instance, how the “store” is updated when an order is executed, or how the “backtest mode” replays historical market data through the entire pipeline.
 • Include annotations (if space allows) such as “plugin interface for exchange drivers” or “modular strategy execution engine” to clarify design choices.
 • Finally, make sure the diagram is detailed enough to represent every main component but also compact enough to be understandable at a glance.

Following these guidelines, the final diagram will present a comprehensive view of Jesse’s modular architecture, tailored to its purpose as an advanced cryptocurrency trading framework. Each major component, relationship, and data flow should be clearly labeled and visually distinct using directional arrows and color-coding to facilitate easy understanding by the team.
</explanation>
